abstract: This NBER working paper develops a labor-search model to examine how artificial intelligence impacts labor productivity and unemployment. AI is conceptualized as a learning-by-using technology that improves through machine learning from workers while simultaneously enhancing their productivity, creating a feedback loop between human labor and AI capability. The model identifies three possible equilibria: no AI adoption, partial AI adoption with elevated joblessness, and widespread AI adoption supporting sustained growth with minimal employment effects. Under the partial-AI equilibrium, the model predicts more than threefold improvements in productivity alongside a long-run employment loss of 23%, with roughly half occurring within five years. The authors find that targeted subsidies for jobs at displacement risk could generate welfare improvements ranging from 26.6% in the short run to over 50% in the long run, providing a strong theoretical case for active labor market intervention.
keyFindings: Three distinct equilibria are possible: no AI adoption, partial AI with elevated unemployment, and widespread AI supporting growth with minimal employment effects — the realized outcome depends on labor market frictions and wage dynamics.
Under partial AI adoption, the model predicts more than threefold productivity improvements alongside 23% long-run employment loss, with roughly half the displacement occurring within five years.
Targeted subsidies for at-risk jobs could generate welfare improvements of 26.6% in the short run to over 50% in the long run, providing strong theoretical support for active labor market policy.
AI functions as a learning-by-using technology — it improves through interaction with workers, creating a feedback loop that makes early adoption decisions consequential for long-run outcomes.
The unbounded-AI scenario with endogenous growth could avoid technological unemployment entirely, but reaching this equilibrium depends on successful wage renegotiation and institutional conditions.
methodology: Theoretical labor-search model calibrated to U.S. labor market data. The model incorporates AI as a learning-by-using technology with endogenous capability improvement, labor market frictions, and wage bargaining dynamics. The authors analyze equilibrium properties, transition dynamics, and policy counterfactuals through numerical simulation.
qualifiers: Primarily theoretical — the specific quantitative predictions (23% employment loss, threefold productivity gains) depend heavily on calibration assumptions and parameter values. The model highlights considerable uncertainty, with potential for global and local indeterminacy across equilibria. The learning-by-using assumption may not accurately characterize all AI deployment modes. Labor-search frictions are stylized and may not capture the full complexity of real-world labor market adjustment.
